title: Relational Model: Tables and Keys
relevance: Campus OAs and SDE interviews routinely test whether you can define keys, distinguish super/candidate/primary keys, and count super keys from a schema.

phases.goal: Establish what a schema/table is and what makes an attribute set a key or candidate key.

must_hit.point: A schema is the logical representation of the data; data is held in tables (relations) of rows and columns.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Says schema is logical structure and tables/relations store the actual rows and columns.

must_hit.point: A key is an attribute or set of attributes whose purpose is to uniquely identify a row (tuple) of a table.
must_hit.evidence_hint: States uniqueness of a row/tuple as the purpose of a key.

must_hit.point: A candidate key is a minimal set of attributes that can uniquely identify every tuple of a relation; a relation may have several candidate keys.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Mentions both uniqueness and minimality, and that multiple candidate keys are allowed.

must_hit.point: SQL's data-definition language (DDL) is the sub-language used to declare tables.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Names DDL as the language for declaring table structure.

probes: What is a candidate key, and how does it differ from just any unique-looking column?
In the Student example with repeating Sname/City/Age, why is Rollno a candidate key and the others not?

hints.1: Think about what lets you pick out exactly one row.
hints.2: Separate uniqueness from minimality — candidate keys need both.
hints.3: A candidate key is a minimal uniquely identifying attribute set; Rollno works because Sname/City/Age repeat across rows.

phases.goal: Explain super keys, how to count them, and how primary and alternate keys are chosen from candidate keys.

must_hit.point: A super key is any combination of attributes that can uniquely identify the tuples of a table; any superset of a candidate key is a super key.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Defines super key as uniquely identifying and notes supersets of candidate keys remain super keys.

must_hit.point: If a relation has n attributes and one single-attribute candidate key, the number of super keys is 2^{n-1}.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Gives 2^{n-1}, optionally illustrating with Rollno/name/age yielding 4 super keys.

must_hit.point: With two single-attribute candidate keys A1 and A2, super keys are counted by inclusion–exclusion as 2^{n-1} + 2^{n-1} - 2^{n-2}.
must_hit.evidence_hint: States the formula and explains subtracting the double-counted subsets containing both keys.

must_hit.point: Among candidate keys the designer selects one primary key; the rest become alternate keys. Primary key means Unique + Not Null.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Says one candidate is promoted to primary, others are alternate, and cites Unique + Not Null.

must_hit.point: Key hierarchy: every primary key is a candidate key, and every candidate key is a super key.
must_hit.evidence_hint: States the inclusion chain PK ⊂ candidate ⊂ super key.

probes: If Rollno is the only candidate key in a 3-attribute relation, how many super keys are there and what are they?
How do you count super keys when there are two single-attribute candidate keys?

hints.1: Start from subsets that contain the whole candidate key.
hints.2: For one single-attribute candidate key, freely include or exclude each of the other n-1 attributes.
hints.3: Answer is 2^{n-1}; for Rollno/name/age that is 4: {Rollno}, {Rollno,name}, {Rollno,age}, {Rollno,name,age}.

phases.goal: Distinguish super keys, candidate keys, and the chosen primary key without conflating the three.

must_hit.point: A super key need not be minimal — {Rollno, name} is a super key but not a candidate key because Rollno alone already suffices.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Gives a non-minimal super key example and says candidate keys must be minimal.

must_hit.point: A candidate key is a minimal super key; the primary key is the chosen candidate key.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Explicitly separates minimality (candidate) from designer choice (primary).

probes: Is {Rollno, name} a candidate key? Why or why not?
What is the difference between a candidate key and the primary key?

hints.1: Ask whether any attribute can be dropped while still uniquely identifying rows.
hints.2: Candidate = minimal super key; primary = the one the designer picks among candidates.
hints.3: {Rollno, name} is a super key but not a candidate key; Rollno alone is the candidate, and primary is whichever candidate is chosen.

phases.goal: Apply the definitions to the Student example and to composite multi-candidate counting.

must_hit.point: In the Student table, Sname, City, and Age repeat across rows (e.g. rows 1 and 3 share Reddy, Hyderabad, 20), so none of those columns can distinguish a row; Rollno is unique and is a candidate key.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Walks the example and rejects non-unique columns while accepting Rollno.

must_hit.point: For two disjoint composite candidate keys {A1,A2} and {A3,A4}, the number of super keys is 2^{n-2} + 2^{n-2} - 2^{n-4}.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Applies inclusion–exclusion to the two pairs and subtracts subsets containing all four attributes.

probes: Using the Student table sample, which attributes can be candidate keys and why?
How do you count super keys if the candidate keys are the disjoint pairs {A1,A2} and {A3,A4}?

hints.1: Look for columns whose values never collide across rows.
hints.2: Count subsets that contain at least one whole candidate key; use inclusion–exclusion when there are several.
hints.3: Only Rollno qualifies in the example; for the two pairs the count is 2^{n-2} + 2^{n-2} - 2^{n-4}.

tradeoffs.strong_answer: Any uniquely identifying attribute set is a super key, including non-minimal ones like {Rollno, name}. A candidate key must be a minimal super key — no proper subset still uniquely identifies tuples.
Both are candidate keys (unique and not null). The designer selects one candidate as the primary key; the remaining candidates are alternate keys.

gotchas.trap: Treating any uniquely identifying set as a candidate key — e.g. calling {Rollno, name} a candidate key.
gotchas.correction: A candidate key must be minimal. {Rollno, name} is a super key but not a candidate key because Rollno alone already suffices.

gotchas.trap: Confusing candidate key with primary key.
gotchas.correction: Every primary key is a candidate key, but not every candidate key is primary — primary is the one chosen; the others are alternate keys.

gotchas.trap: Counting super keys as all 2^n subsets, or forgetting inclusion–exclusion with multiple candidate keys.
gotchas.correction: Count only subsets that contain at least one whole candidate key. One single-attribute candidate key gives 2^{n-1}; for several candidates, apply inclusion–exclusion (e.g. 2^{n-1}+2^{n-1}-2^{n-2} for two single-attribute keys).
